paragraphs.heading: A pile of loose fragments
paragraphs.text: A cinder cone, also called a scoria cone, is a steep, cone-shaped landform built around a volcanic vent. It is made of loose pyroclastic fragments, for example volcanic ash, clinkers or scoria. Most have a bowl-shaped crater at the top. They range from tens to hundreds of metres tall.

paragraphs.heading: What the fragments are like
paragraphs.text: The material in a cinder cone is loose, and that sets it apart from a spatter cone, which is made of agglomerated volcanic bombs. The fragments are usually basaltic to andesitic in composition. They are often glassy and hold many gas bubbles, frozen in place when magma exploded into the air and cooled quickly. Cinder cone eruptions also commonly produce volcanic bombs, which are lava fragments larger than 64 mm across.

paragraphs.heading: Four stages of growth
paragraphs.text: A cinder cone's growth may be divided into four stages. In the first, a ring of scoria with a low rim forms. In the second, the rim grows higher and a talus slope starts to form outside it. In the third, slumping and blasts destroy the original rim. In the fourth, talus builds up beyond the ballistic zone, which is the zone where cinder falls to the surface.

paragraphs.heading: Why lava comes out at the base
paragraphs.text: Late in an eruption the magma has lost most of its gas. It no longer fountains. It oozes quietly as lava into the crater or under the cone's base. Lava rarely comes out of the top, because the loose cinders are too weak to hold the pressure of molten rock rising through the central vent. With so few gas bubbles, the lava is denser than the bubble-rich cinders, so it often burrows out along the bottom of the cone, lifting the cinders like corks on water, and spreads outward as a lava flow around the base. When the eruption ends, a symmetrical cone sits in the middle of a pad of lava.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: Of all volcano types, basaltic cinder cones are the one most characteristic of intraplate volcanism. Cinder cones are common, too, on the flanks of shield volcanoes, of stratovolcanoes and of calderas. Geologists have identified nearly 100 of them on the flanks of Mauna Kea, a shield volcano on the island of Hawaii.

paragraphs.heading: Cones that erupt only once
paragraphs.text: Some cinder cones are monogenetic, which means they form in one short eruptive episode that yields a very small volume of lava. The eruption typically lasts just weeks or months, though occasionally fifteen years or longer. Such cones likely form when magma is supplied to a volcanic field at a very low rate and eruptions are spread out in space and time. No one eruption then sets up a system of "plumbing" that would give later eruptions an easy path up, so each must find its own way to the surface. Not all cinder cones are like this. Some ancient ones show intervals of soil formation between flows, a sign that eruptions were thousands to tens of thousands of years apart.

paragraphs.heading: Famous cones, here and on Mars
paragraphs.text: Paricutin, the most famous cinder cone, grew from a new vent in a Mexican corn field in 1943. Its eruptions went on for nine years, built the cone 424 metres high and produced lava flows covering 25 km². Cerro Negro in Nicaragua is Earth's most historically active cinder cone, with more than 20 eruptions since its first in 1850. On Mars, cinder cones seem to be more than two times wider than those on Earth, as lower atmospheric pressure and gravity let ejected particles spread over a larger area.
